newsitem.title: USA: Leaf rust seen posing yield risk to U.S. HRW wheat.
newsitem.headline: Leaf rust seen posing yield risk to U.S. HRW wheat.

text.p: Current levels of leaf rust fungus in southern U.S. Plains wheat may foreshadow significant yield reductions in the U.S. hard red winter wheat crop, plant pathologists said Tuesday.

"The leaf rust is increasing down in south Texas and central Texas...on susceptible plants, and it could possibly be another leaf rust year like 1992/93 when we did see losses in Kansas of 10 percent or more," said Dave Long, plant pathologist at the USDA Agricultural Research Service's (ARS) Cereal Rust Lab in St. Paul, Minnesota.

Leaf rust reduces wheat quality by lowering protein concentration in the grain. If it occurs early enough in the growing cycle, it can also cut off the plant's ability to nourish itself, thereby reducing yields.

Long said the degree of leaf rust at this time of the year in Texas is usually a sign of how serious the epidemic will become later in the spring in key wheat growing regions of Kansas and northern Oklahoma.
That's because air currents usually carry the rust spores north, and they are subsequently deposited on wheat fields by rains, Long said.

Merle Eversmeyer, ARS plant pathologist in Manhattan, Kansas, returned Monday from his annual tour of Texas, Oklahoma and southern Kansas, during which he gauged the presence of leaf rust in the wheat crop.
"I'm finding the same level of leaf rust there, especially in southern Texas, that I did in 1992/93 and 1993/94," Eversmeyer told Reuters Tuesday.

But Eversmeyer warned that although leaf rust levels in the southern Plains usually indicate what will develop in the central Plains, the extent of the leaf rust epidemic will hinge on weather conditions over the next month.
"The potential for the (rust) to move in is great," Eversmeyer said. "What's going to happen is going to depend upon the weather conditions that we have from here on."

Eversmeyer said a severe frost could burn back the leaves on the wheat plants, thereby killing off rust spores. Dry weather would also halt the rust epidemic, although it might starve the plants of needed water during the growing season.

If rust were to take hold in Kansas and Oklahoma, some individual fields could suffer yield losses of 20 to 30 percent, Eversmeyer said. But other fields planted with rust resistant varieties may suffer negligible losses, he said.
The weekly crop weather report released Monday by Texas Agricultural Statistics reported that rust was beginning to show up in fields in the Blacklands of north central Texas.

Rust was fairly widespread last fall in Kansas, but Eversmeyer explained that much of it did not live through the winter. He estimated that the fungus was present on one percent of Kansas winter wheat acreage, but he cautioned that this was still a significant amount.
"At this early stage, even if you only have one plant in a hundred that has a pustule on it, you have potential for a severe (outbreak)," Eversmeyer said.
Eversmeyer said that by April 20 he will have a clearer idea of just how widespread the epidemic is in Kansas and how much wheat is at risk.

Long, who next week will release his first report of the season on the rust situation, also said sources had told him that the fungus had developed in Georgia and Louisiana and could threaten the soft red winter wheat crop there.
